Since <math>\rho^m = \left(1+\frac{x}{m}\right)^m \left\{1+\frac{y^2}{m(\sqrt{m}+x/\sqrt{m})^2}\right\}^{\frac{1}{2}m}</math>, we have <math>\lim_{m=\infty}\rho^m = e^x. \lim_{m=\infty} \left\{1+\frac{y^2}{m(\sqrt{m}+x/\sqrt{m})^2}\right\}^{\frac{1}{2}m}</math>. Let <math>r</math> be a fixed number less than <math>\sqrt{m}+x/\sqrt{m}</math>, then <math>\lim_{m=\infty} \left\{1+\frac{y^2}{m(\sqrt{m}+x\sqrt{m})^2}\right\}^{\frac{1}{2}m}</math> lies between 1 and <math>\lim_{m=\infty} \left\{1+\frac{y^2}{mr^2}\right\}^{\frac{1}{2}m}</math>, or between 1 and <math>e^{y^2/2r^2}</math>; hence since <math>r</math> can be taken arbitrarily large, the limit is 1. The limit of <math>m\phi</math> or <math>m \tan^{-1}\{y/(x+m)\}</math> is the same as that of <math>my/(x+m)</math> which is <math>y</math>. Hence we have shown that <math>E(z) = e^x(\cos y+i \sin y)</math>.

21. ''Exponential Values of Trigonometrical Functions.'' Since <math>E(x+iy) = i^x(\cos y+\sin y</math>, we have <math>\cos y+i \sin y = E(iy)</math>, and <math>\cos y-i \sin y = E(-iy)</math>. Therefore <math>\cos y = \tfrac{1}{2}\{E(iy) + E(-iy)\}</math>, <math>\sin y = \tfrac{1}{2}i\{E(iy)-E(-iy)\}</math>; and using the series defined by <math>E(iy)</math> and <math>E(-iy)</math>, we find that <math>\cos y = 1 - y^2/2! + y^4/4! - \dots</math>, <math>\sin y = y - y^3/3! + y^5/5! - \dots</math>, where <math>y</math> is any real number. These are the well-known expansions of <math>\cos y</math>, <math>\sin y</math> in powers of the circular measure <math>y</math>. Where <math>z</math> is a complex number, the symbol <math>e^z</math> may be defined to be such that its ''principal value'' is <math>E(z)</math>; thus the principal values of <math>e^{iy}</math>, <math>e^{-iy}</math> are <math>E(iy)</math>, <math>E(-iy)</math>. The above expressions for <math>\cos y</math>, <math>\sin y</math> may then be written <math>\cos y = \tfrac{1}{2}(e^{iy}+e^{-iy})</math>, <math>\sin y = \tfrac{1}{2}i(e^{iy}-e^{-iy})</math>. These are known as the exponential values of the cosine and sine. It can be shown that the symbol <math>e^z</math> as defined here satisfies the usual laws of combination for exponents.

Let <math>r</math> be a fixed number less than <math>\sqrt{m}+x/\sqrt{m}</math>, then <math>\lim_{m=\infty} \left\{1+\frac{y^2}{m(\sqrt{m}+x\sqrt{m})^2}\right\}^{\frac{1}{2}m}</math> lies between 1 and <math>\lim_{m=\infty} \left\{1+\frac{y^2}{mr^2}\right\}^{\frac{1}{2}m}</math>, or between 1 and <math>e^{y^2/2r^2}</math>; hence since <math>r</math> can be taken arbitrarily large, the limit is 1. 21. ''Exponential Values of Trigonometrical Functions.'' Since <math>E(x+iy) = i^x(\cos y+\sin y</math>, we have <math>\cos y+i \sin y = E(iy)</math>, and <math>\cos y-i \sin y = E(-iy)</math>. Therefore <math>\cos y = \tfrac{1}{2}\{E(iy) + E(-iy)\}</math>, <math>\sin y = \tfrac{1}{2}i\{E(iy)-E(-iy)\}</math>; and using the series defined by <math>E(iy)</math> and <math>E(-iy)</math>, we find that <math>\cos y = 1 - y^2/2! + y^4/4! - \dots</math>, <math>\sin y = y - y^3/3! + y^5/5! - \dots</math>, where <math>y</math> is any real number. These are the well-known expansions of <math>\cos y</math>, <math>\sin y</math> in powers of the circular measure <math>y</math>. Where <math>z</math> is a complex number, the symbol <math>e^z</math> may be defined to be such that its ''principal value'' is <math>E(z)</math>; thus the principal values of <math>e^{iy}</math>, <math>e^{-iy}</math> are <math>E(iy)</math>, <math>E(-iy)</math>. The above expressions for <math>\cos y</math>, <math>\sin y</math> may then be written <math>\cos y = \tfrac{1}{2}(e^{iy}+e^{-iy})</math>, <math>\sin y = \tfrac{1}{2}i(e^{iy}-e^{-iy})</math>. These are known as the exponential values of the cosine and sine. It can be shown that the symbol <math>e^z</math> as defined here satisfies the usual laws of combination for exponents.

22. '''''Analytical Definitions of Trigonometrical Functions.''''' The two functions <math>\cos z</math>, <math>\sin z</math> may be defined for all complex or real values of <math>z</math> by means of the equations <math>\cos y = \tfrac{1}{2}\{E(z) + E(-z)\}</math>, <math>\sin z = (\tfrac{1}{2i})\{E(z) - E(-z)\}</math>, where <math>\text{E}(z)</math> represents the sum-function of <math>1 + z + z^2/2! + \dots + z^n/n! + \dots</math> For real values of <math>z</math> this is in accordance with the ordinary definitions, as appears from the series obtained above for <math>\cos y</math>, <math>\sin y</math>. The fundamental properties of <math>\cos z</math>, <math>\sin z</math> can be deduced from this definition. Thus <math>\cos z + i \sin z = E(z)</math>, <math>\cos z - i \sin z = E(-iz)</math>; therefore <math>\cos^2 z + \sin^2 z = E(iz) . E(-iz) = 1</math>. Again <math>\cos (z_1 + z_2)</math> is given by <math>\tfrac{1}{2}\{E(iz_1 + iz_2) + E(-iz_1 - iz_2)\} = \tfrac{1}{2}\{E(iz_1)E(iz_2) + E(-iz_1)E(-iz_2)\}</math> or <math>\tfrac{1}{4}\{E(iz_1) + E(-iz_1)\}\{E(iz_2) + E(-iz_2)\} + \tfrac{1}{4}\{E(iz_1) - E(-iz_1)\}\{E(iz_2) - E(-iz_2)\}</math>, whence we have <math>\cos (z_1 + z_2) = \cos z_1 \cos z_2 - \sin z_1 \sin z_2</math>. Similarly, we find that <math>\sin (z_1 + z_2) = \sin z_1 \cos z_2 + \cos z_1 \sin z_2</math>. Again the equation <math>E(z) = 1</math> has no real roots except <math>z = 0</math>, for <math>e^y > 1</math>, if <math>z</math> is real and <math>> 0</math>. Also <math>\text{E}(z) = 1</math> has no complex root <math>\alpha + i\beta</math>, for <math>\alpha - i\beta</math> would then also be a root, and <math>E(2\alpha) = E(\alpha + i\beta)E(\alpha - i\beta) = 1</math>, which is impossible unless <math>\alpha = 0</math>. The roots of <math>E(z) = 1</math> are therefore purely imaginary (except <math>z = 0</math>); the smallest numerically we denote by <math>2\ i\pi</math>, so that <math>E(2i\pi) = 1</math>. We have then <math>E(2i\pi r) = \{E(2i\pi)\}^r = 1</math>, if <math>r</math> is any integer; therefore <math>2i\pi r</math> is a root. It can be shown that no root lies between <math>2i\pi r</math> and <math>2(r + 1)i\pi</math>; and thus that all the roots are given by <math>z = \pm 2i\pi r</math>. Since <math>E(y + 2i\pi) = E(z)E(2i\pi) = E(z)</math>, we see that <math>E(z)</math> is periodic, of period <math>2i\pi</math>. It follows that <math>\cos z</math>, <math>\sin z</math> are periodic, of periods <math>2\pi</math>. The number here introduced may be identified with the ratio of the circumference to the diameter of a circle by considering the case of real values of <math>z</math>.

23. '''''Expansion of Powers of Sines and Cosines''''' Consider the binomial theorem
{{block center|<math>(a + b)^n = a^n + na^{n-1}b + \frac{n(n - 1)}{2!} a^{n-2}b^2 + \dots</math>}}
{{block center|<math>+ \frac{n(n - 1) \dots (n - r + 1)}{r!} a^{n-r}b^r + \dots + b^n.</math>}} '''''in Series of Sines and Cosines of Multiple Arc.''''' Putting <math>a=e^{\iota\theta}</math>, <math>b=e^{-\iota\theta}</math>, we obtain
{{block center|<math>(2\cos\theta)^n=2\cos n\theta+n2\cos\overline{n-2\theta}</math>}}
{{block center|<math>+\frac{n(n-1)}{2\,!}2\cos\overline{n-4\theta}+\dots</math>}}
{{block center|<math>+\frac{n(n-1)\dots(n-r+1)}{r\,!}2\cos(n-2r)\theta+\dots</math>}}
When <math>n</math> is odd the last term is <math>2\frac{n(n-1)\dots\frac{1}{2}(n+3)}{\frac{1}{2}(n-1)\,!}\cos\theta</math>, and when <math>n</math> is even it is <math>\frac{n(n-1)\dots(\frac{1}{2}n+1)}{\frac{1}{2}n\,!}</math>.

If we put <math>a=e^{\iota\theta}</math>, <math>b=-e^{-\iota\theta}</math>, we obtain the formula
{{block center|<math>(-1)^{\frac{1}{2}n}(2\sin\theta)^n=2\cos n\theta-2n\cos(n-2)\theta+\frac{n(n-1)}{1.2}2\cos(n-4)\theta-\dots</math>}}
{{block center|<math>+(-1)^{n-r}\frac{n(n-1)\dots(n-r+1)}{r\,!}2\cos(n-2r)\theta\dots</math>}}
{{block center|<math>+(-1)^{\frac{n}{2}}\frac{n(n-1)\dots(\frac{1}{2}n+1)}{\frac{1}{2}n\,!}</math>}}
when <math>n</math> is even, and
{{block center|<math>(-1)^{\frac{1}{2}(n-1)}(2\sin\theta)^n=2\sin n\theta-n\,.\,2\sin(n-2)\theta+\frac{n(n-1)}{1.2}2\sin(n-4)\theta\dots</math>}}
{{block center|<math>+(-)^{\frac{n-1}{2}}\frac{n(n-1)\dots\frac{1}{2}(n+3)}{\frac{1}{2}(n-1)\,!}\sin\theta</math>}} when <math>n</math> is odd. These formulae enable us to express any positive integral power of the sine or cosine in terms of sines or cosines of multiples of the argument. There are corresponding formulae when <math>n</math> is not a positive integer.

''Expansion of Sines and Cosines of Multiple Arcs in Powers of Sines and Cosines of Arc.'' Consider the identity <math>\log(1-px)+\log(1-qx)=\log(1-\overline{p+q}x+pqx^2)</math>. Expand both sides of this equation in powers of <math>x</math>, and equate the coefficients of <math>x^n</math>, we then get
{{block center|<math>p^n+q^n=(p+q)^n-n(p+q)^{n-2}pq</math>}}
{{block center|<math>+\frac{n(n-3)}{2!}(p+q)^{n-4}p^2q^2+\dots</math>}}
{{block center|<math>+(-1)^r\frac{n(n-r-1)(n-r-2)\dots(n-2r+1)}{r!}</math>}}
{{block center|<math>(p+q)^{n-2r}p^rq^r+\dots</math>}}
If we write this series in the reverse order, we have
{{block center|<math>p^n+q^n=2(-1)^{\frac{n}{2}}\Big[(pq)^{\frac{n}{2}}-\frac{n^2}{2!}(pq)^{\frac{n}{2}-1}\left(\frac{p+q}{2}\right)^2</math>}}
{{block center|<math>+\frac{n^2(n^2-2^2)}{4!}(pq)^{\frac{n}{2}-2}\left(\frac{p+q}{2}\right)^4</math>}}
{{block center|<math>-\frac{n^2(n^2-2^2)(n^2-4^2)}{6!}(pq)^{\frac{n}{2}-3}\left(\frac{p+q}{2}\right)^6+\dots+(-1)^{\frac{n}{2}}\tfrac{1}{2}(p+q)^n\Big]</math>}}
when <math>n</math> is even, and
{{block center|<math>p^n+q^n=2(-1)^{\frac{n-1}{2}}\Big[n(pq)^{\frac{n-1}{2}}\left(\frac{p+q}{2}\right)-\frac{n(n^2-1^2)}{3!}(pq)^{\frac{n-3}{2}}\left(\frac{p+q}{2}\right)^3</math>}}
{{block center|<math>+\frac{n(n^2-1^2)(n^2-3^2)}{5!}(pq)^{\frac{n-5}{2}}\left(\frac{p+q}{2}\right)^5+\dots+(-1)^{\frac{n-1}{2}}\tfrac{1}{2}(p+q)^n\Big]</math>}} when <math>n</math> is odd. If in these three formulae we put <math>p=e^{\iota\theta}</math>, <math>q=e^{-\iota\theta}</math>, we obtain the following series for <math>\cos n\theta</math>:—
{{block center|<math>2\cos n\theta=(2\cos\theta)^n-n(2\cos\theta)^{n-2}+\frac{n(n-3)}{2!}(2\cos\theta)^{n-4}-\dots</math>}}
{{block center|<math>+(-1)^r\frac{n(n-r-1)(n-r-2)\dots(n-2r+1)}{r!}(2\cos\theta)^{n-2r}+\dots</math> (7)}}
when <math>n</math> is any positive integer;
{{block center|<math>(-1)^{\frac{n}{2}}\cos u\theta=1-\frac{n^2}{2!}\cos^2\theta+\frac{n^2(n^2-2^2)}{4!}\cos^4\theta-\frac{n^2(n^2-2^2)(n^2-4^2)}{6!}\cos^6\theta</math>}}
{{block center|<math>+\dots+(-1)^{\frac{n}{2}}2^{n-1}\cos^n\theta</math> (8)}}
when <math>n</math> is an even positive integer;
{{block center|<math>(-1)^{\frac{n-1}{2}}\cos n\theta=n\cos n\theta-\frac{n(n^2-1^2)}{3!}\cos^3\theta+\frac{n(n^2-1^2)(n^2-3^2)}{5!}\cos^5\theta-</math>}}
{{block center|<math>\dots+(-1)^{\frac{n-1}{2}}2^{n-1}\cos^n\theta</math> (9)}}
when <math>n</math> is odd. If in the same three formulae we put <math>p=e^{\iota\theta}</math>, <math>q=-e^{-\iota\theta}</math>, we obtain the following four formulae:—
{{block center|<math>(-1)^{\frac{n}{2}}2\cos n\theta=(2\sin\theta)^n-n(2\sin\theta)^{n-2}+\frac{n(n-3)}{2!}(2\sin\theta)^{n-4}-\dots</math>}}
{{block center|<math>+(-1)^r\frac{n(n-r-1)\dots(n-2r-1)}{r!}(2\sin\theta)^{n-2r}+\dots</math> (<math>n</math> even); (10)}}
{{block center|<math>(-1)^{\frac{n-1}{2}}2\sin n\theta=</math>the same series (<math>n</math> odd); (11)}}
{{block center|<math>\cos n\theta=1-\frac{n^2}{2!}\sin^2\theta+\frac{n^2(n^2-2^2)}{4!}\sin^4\theta-\frac{n^2(n^2-2^2)(n^2-4^2)}{6!}\sin^6\theta</math>}}
{{block center|<math>+\dots+2^{n-1}\sin^n\theta</math> (<math>n</math> even); (12) <math>\sin n\theta = n \sin \theta - \frac{n(n^2 - 1^2)}{3\,!} \sin^3\theta + \frac{n(n^2 - 1^2)(n^2 - 3^2)}{5\,!} \sin^5\theta - \dots</math>}}
{{block center|<math>+(-1)^{\frac{n-1}{2}} 2^{n-1} \sin^n\theta\ (n \text{ odd}).</math> (13)}}

Next consider the identity <math>\frac{p}{1 - px} - \frac{q}{1 - qx} = \frac{p - q}{1 - (p + q)x + pqx^2}.</math> Expand both sides of this equation in powers of <math>x</math>, and equate the coefficients of <math>x^{n-1}</math>, then we obtain the equation
{{block center|<math>\frac{p^n - q^n}{p - q} = (p + q)^{n-1} - (n - 2)(p + q)^{n-3}\,pq</math>}}
{{block center|<math>+ \frac{(n - 3)(n - 4)}{2\,!}\,(p + q)^{n-5}\,p^2q^2 - \dots</math>}}
{{block center|<math>\cdots\ (-1)^r \frac{(n - r - 1)\,(n - r - 2) \dots (n - 2r)}{r\,!}\,(p + q)^{n-2r-1}\,p^r q^r + \dots</math>}}
If, as before, we write this in the reverse order, we have the series
{{block center|<math>(-1)^{\frac{n}{2}-1} \Bigg[ n \left(\frac{p + q}{2}\right) (pq)^{\frac{n}{2}-1} - \frac{n(n^2 - 2^2)}{3\,!} \left(\frac{p + q}{2}\right)^3 (pq)^{\frac{n}{2}-3}</math>}}
{{block center|<math>+ \frac{n(n^2 - 2^2)(n^2 - 4^2)}{5\,!} \left(\frac{p + q}{2}\right)^5 (pq)^{\frac{n}{2}-5} + \dots + (-1)^{\frac{n}{2}-1} (p + q)^{n-1} \Bigg]</math>}}<noinclude><references/></noinclude>
